Know your productsFour jobs

Four jobs your money can do

Read from left to right. Each job works best once the one before it is in place: protection before investing, and a core portfolio before specialist strategies.

Before you move rightTick what is already in place

  • Term cover that matches your family’s needs, often 10 to 15 times yearly income
  • Health cover for every member of your family, not only through an employer
  • An emergency fund of about six months’ expenses, easy to reach
  • A core portfolio in mutual funds or SIFs, linked to your goals

PRIM is the mutual-fund-only PMS route that starts on 1 April 2027. Insurance is priced by premium and GIFT City minimums are in US dollars, so neither is on the scale above.

Term Insurance

Pure life cover for your family · regulated by IRDAI

Term insurance keeps your family’s plans on track if you are not there to provide for them. You pay a premium each year, and if something happens to you during the term, your family receives the full cover amount.

How to recognise it

  • Replaces your income for your family, so loans, school fees and monthly expenses stay covered.
  • The premium is fixed when you buy and usually stays the same for the whole term.
  • Your family can receive the amount at once, as a monthly income, or both, as you choose.

Often confused with

Return-of-premium and endowment plans. They give money back at the end, but cost much more for the same cover. Some term plans offer a ‘special exit’ instead: stop at a set age and get your base premiums back.

4Facts as of October 2026
01 · Term insuranceProtect
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
IRDAI
What you pay
A premium, yearly or monthly, fixed when you buy. It depends on your age, health, habits, cover and term.
Time commitment
The term you choose, usually until your earning years end (age 60–70). You get 30 days to return a new policy (free look).
When it pays
To your family (your nominee) if something happens to you during the term. IRDAI allows 15 days to settle a claim, or 45 if it needs investigation.
Costs
Only the premium. No GST on individual policies since 22 September 2025.
Tax in brief
Old regime: premium deductible under Sec. 123 (earlier 80C). The amount your family receives is tax-free.

Work out your coverRule of thumb: 10 to 15 times yearly income

AYearly household expenses₹
D+ Loans still to repay₹
B× Years your family needs support
E+ Big goals: education, marriage₹
C= Income to replace (A × B)₹
F− Savings and existing cover₹
Cover you need = C + D + E − F₹

Suits you if

  • Your family depends on your income, now or in the years ahead.
  • You have a home loan or other commitments your family would carry.
  • You want the largest cover for the lowest premium.

Think twice if

  • No one depends on your income and you have no loans.
  • You want money back at the end. That is a savings goal; keep it separate.
  • You are not ready to share your full health details. Honest disclosure keeps claims smooth.

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • Is the cover enough for my family’s plans, including my loans?
  • Have I shared every health detail, habit and existing policy?
  • Who is my nominee, and does my family know about this policy?
  • What is the insurer’s claim settlement record?

Health Insurance

Hospital cover for your family · regulated by IRDAI

You pay a premium every year. If you need hospital treatment, the insurer pays the bills up to your sum insured, directly to the hospital (cashless) or by repaying you, so the focus stays on getting better.

How to recognise it

  • Pays actual hospital bills up to the sum insured, for one person or the whole family (floater).
  • Claim-free years can raise your cover (no-claim bonus). Some policies refill cover used up in a year (restoration).
  • You can move to another insurer without losing waiting-period credit (portability).

Often confused with

Critical illness cover. Pays a fixed lump sum when a listed illness is diagnosed, whatever the bill. It adds to health insurance; it does not replace it.

Employer cover. Usually ends when you change jobs or retire.

6Facts as of October 2026
02 · Health insuranceProtect
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
IRDAI
What you pay
A yearly premium based on age, sum insured, city and health history. No upper age limit to buy since April 2024; insurers still assess each applicant.
Time commitment
One year at a time. Renew without a break to keep waiting-period credit and bonus.
When it pays
Cashless at network hospitals (the insurer must decide within 1 hour of a request, and approve discharge within 3 hours), or by reimbursement.
Costs
Only the premium. No GST on individual policies since 22 September 2025.
Tax in brief
Old regime: premium deductible under Sec. 126 (earlier 80D), up to ₹25,000 (₹50,000 for senior citizens), plus a separate limit for parents.

Read the fine printCompare before you buy

TermLook forWatch out for
Room rentNo cap, or any single private roomA daily cap. Go above it and the whole bill can be cut in proportion.
Co-paymentNoneYou pay a fixed share of every claim
Sub-limitsNoneCaps on treatments such as cataract or knee surgery
RestorationCover refills if used up in a yearNo refill
Waiting periodsShort, or reducible with an add-onThe full 3 years for conditions you already have

Suits you if

  • A large hospital bill would eat into your savings.
  • Your only cover today comes from your employer.
  • You have parents or senior family members to look after.

Think twice if

  • You are buying mainly for the tax deduction.
  • You have not checked the room-rent cap, co-payment and sub-limits.
  • You plan to let a policy lapse to switch insurers. Port it instead.

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • Is there a room-rent cap or a co-payment?
  • Which hospitals near me offer cashless treatment?
  • Which of my conditions have a waiting period, and how long is it?
  • Is the sum insured enough for hospital costs in my city?

Mutual Funds

Pooled, professionally managed · regulated by SEBI

Many investors pool their money. A professional fund manager invests it in shares, bonds, gold or other assets, as the scheme’s rules allow. You own units of the pool, and their value (the NAV) is published every business day.

How to recognise it

  • You own units of a pool, not the shares or bonds themselves.
  • Every scheme has a Direct plan and a Regular plan. A Regular plan includes the distributor’s commission.
  • Schemes must stay true to their label: a large-cap fund, for example, keeps at least 80% in large companies.

Often confused with

SIF. Run by mutual fund houses with the same tax rules, plus tools for falling and sideways markets. Read it next: entry 04.

ULIP. An insurance policy with an investment part, regulated by IRDAI. It is not a mutual fund.

8Facts as of October 2026
03 · Mutual fundsBuild
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
SEBI. AMFI is the industry body.
Minimum
Set by each scheme. SIPs often start at ₹100–₹500 a month.
Time commitment
None for most open-ended funds. Tax-saving ELSS funds lock in for 3 years. Equity funds suit goals 5+ years away.
Money out
Sell units any business day. An exit load may apply if you leave early.
Costs
The total expense ratio (TER), taken daily from the NAV and capped by SEBI.
Tax in brief
Equity funds: 12.5% on long-term gains (held over 12 months) above ₹1.25 lakh a year; 20% if short-term. Debt funds: your slab rate.

Risk check: the riskometerPrinted on every scheme

Suits you if

  • You are starting out, or want a core portfolio for long-term goals.
  • You want diversification and professional management with small amounts.
  • You like investing a fixed amount every month (SIP).

Think twice if

  • You need guaranteed returns or capital protection.
  • You may need the money within a year. Equity funds can fall sharply.
  • You are picking a fund on last year’s return alone.

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • What is the riskometer level, and does it match my comfort?
  • What are the expense ratio and the exit load?
  • How does this fund fit with what I already own?
  • Direct or Regular plan: what am I paying for, and what do I get?

SIF

Specialised investment funds · regulated by SEBI

A SIF is a mutual fund with a bigger toolkit. It is run by a mutual fund house under SEBI’s mutual fund rules and taxed the same way, but the manager can also bet on falls, move between asset classes, and turn market exposure up or down.

How to recognise it

  • Built for rising, falling and sideways markets: the manager can raise or cut exposure, and bet on falls for up to 25% of the fund.
  • Taxed like a mutual fund: no tax inside the fund, only when you redeem.
  • Can be conservative or adventurous, from arbitrage-and-debt strategies to equity long-short. The Risk Band (Level 1 to 5) tells you which.

Often confused with

Mutual funds. Same family, same tax rules. A SIF adds tools for falling and sideways markets, and starts at ₹10 lakh.

Category III AIFs and PMS. Similar long-short tools, but taxed every year. A SIF defers tax until you redeem. More on the next spread.

10Facts as of October 2026
04 · SIFBuild
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
SEBI, under the mutual fund regulations, through eligible fund houses.
Minimum
₹10 lakh per investor, across one fund house’s SIF strategies.
Time commitment
No lock-in for most strategies. Some are interval or close-ended.
Money out
Equity strategies usually any business day. Hybrid strategies on set days (at least twice a week), with up to 15 working days’ notice.
Costs
An expense ratio taken from the NAV, as with mutual funds.
Tax in brief
Same as mutual funds. Equity-oriented strategies: 12.5% on long-term gains above ₹1.25 lakh (after 12 months), 20% if sooner.

Tax check: why the wrapper mattersHighest tax bracket, illustration

Suits you if

  • You invest in mutual funds and want strategies that can also manage falls and flat markets.
  • You want one fund that can be a complete portfolio, or its steadier part.
  • You prefer mutual-fund tax treatment to AIF or PMS taxation.

Think twice if

  • ₹10 lakh would be most of your investable money.
  • You must be able to withdraw on any day without notice.
  • You expect gains every month. These strategies manage risk; they cannot remove it.

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • Which strategy is this, and what is its Risk Band today?
  • How does the manager change exposure as markets rise, fall or drift?
  • Is it equity-oriented for tax, and how often can I redeem?
  • What are the total costs?

12Facts as of October 2026
04 in depth · SIFBuild

SIF in depth

Using SIFs in your portfolio

Three ways to use a SIFMixes shown are examples

As your whole portfolio

No mutual funds yet? An asset allocator strategy can hold shares, bonds, gold, silver and REITs in one fund, and shift between them.

As the conservative part

Hybrid and debt strategies can keep most money in arbitrage and bonds, with a small share in stocks, aiming for smaller swings than equity funds.

As the equity part

Equity long-short strategies can sit beside your equity funds, and can hedge or cut exposure when markets turn.

Tax in practice: when the tax is paidSame trades, three wrappers

Gains made inside a SIF are not taxed along the way, so that money stays invested until you redeem, and you choose when. Rates are in the tax check in entry 04.

NCDs

Non-convertible debentures · regulated by SEBI

An NCD is a loan you give a company for a fixed period. The company pays you interest at a fixed rate and returns your money at maturity. It can never turn into shares, hence “non-convertible”.

How to recognise it

  • Fixed interest, paid monthly, yearly or all at maturity (cumulative).
  • Carries a credit rating from an agency such as CRISIL, ICRA, CARE or India Ratings.
  • Secured NCDs are backed by the company’s assets. Unsecured ones are not, and rank lower if the company fails.

Often confused with

Bank fixed deposits. Bank deposits are insured up to ₹5 lakh per depositor per bank by DICGC. NCDs are not insured. A higher NCD rate is payment for taking more risk.

14Facts as of October 2026
05 · NCDsBuild
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
SEBI (issue and listing). Issuers that are NBFCs are also regulated by RBI.
Minimum
Usually ₹10,000 in a public issue.
Time commitment
The tenure of the series you pick, usually 18 months to 10 years.
Money out
Interest as chosen, principal at maturity. You can sell earlier on the exchange, but the price may be lower and buyers few.
Costs
No fee to apply in a public issue. A demat account is needed; brokerage applies if you sell.
Tax in brief
Interest is taxed at your slab rate. Selling a listed NCD after 12 months: 12.5% on the gain; earlier, your slab rate.

Risk check: the credit ratingRead it before the interest rate

Suits you if

  • You want a predictable, regular income.
  • You can hold the NCD until it matures.
  • You accept that your money depends on the company’s ability to pay.

Think twice if

  • You are chasing the highest rate. High rates usually mean higher risk.
  • You may need the money before maturity.
  • The NCD is unrated, unsecured, or from a company you do not know.

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • What is the rating, from which agency, and is the outlook stable?
  • Is it secured, and what is the asset cover?
  • Which series: tenure, payout frequency and effective yield?
  • What happens if I need my money early?

PMS

Portfolio management services · regulated by SEBI

A SEBI-registered portfolio manager runs a portfolio of stocks or bonds for you. Unlike a mutual fund, the securities sit in your own demat account, so you can see every holding and every trade.

How to recognise it

  • The shares sit in your own demat account, so you see every holding and every trade.
  • Every PMS reports returns against a common benchmark, so managers can be compared.
  • Upfront fees are not allowed. Fees are fixed, linked to performance above a hurdle, or both.

Often confused with

Mutual funds. A shared pool. You own units, not shares.

AIFs. A pooled fund with a ₹1 crore minimum that can hold unlisted assets and lock you in for years.

16Facts as of October 2026
06 · PMSSpecialise
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
SEBI. The Portfolio Managers Regulations, 2026 apply from 1 April 2027.
Minimum
₹50 lakh. PRIM (mutual-fund-only route): ₹25 lakh from 1 April 2027.
Time commitment
No lock-in. Exit charges may apply in the early years.
Money out
Withdraw part or all. You receive cash, or the securities themselves.
Costs
Management fee and/or performance fee, plus brokerage, custody and GST.
Tax in brief
Every trade is taxed in your hands, as if you had made it yourself.

Risk check: concentrationFewer stocks, bigger bets

Suits you if

  • You have ₹50 lakh or more for equities and want a focused approach.
  • You want to see every stock and trade in your own account.
  • You accept that returns can differ widely from the index.

Think twice if

  • Low cost matters most to you. Compare fees with mutual funds.
  • You would rather not see many capital-gains entries in your tax return.
  • You are choosing a manager on last year’s return alone.

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • How has the strategy done against its benchmark over a full market cycle?
  • What are all the fees: fixed, performance, hurdle, high-water mark, exit?
  • Is the service discretionary or non-discretionary?
  • How many stocks will I hold, and of what size?

AIF

Alternative investment funds · regulated by SEBI

An AIF is a privately pooled fund that reaches where public markets cannot: companies in the years before they list, private credit, real estate and start-ups, as well as specialist strategies in listed markets.

How to recognise it

  • Gives you a share of companies in their private years, often a decade or more before they list.
  • You commit an amount, and the manager draws it in parts (capital calls) as deals are found.
  • Offered only by private placement, to at most 1,000 investors per scheme.

Often confused with

PMS. Your own account, mostly listed shares, and no lock-in. An AIF pools money and may hold assets that cannot be sold quickly.

18Facts as of October 2026
07 · AIFSpecialise
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
SEBI (Alternative Investment Funds Regulations, 2012).
Minimum
₹1 crore commitment, drawn in parts as the fund invests.
Time commitment
Category I and II: closed-ended, often 4–10 years. Category III: open or closed-ended.
Money out
Usually as the fund sells investments, towards the end of its life. Early exit is limited or not possible.
Costs
A management fee plus carried interest, a share of profits above the hurdle.
Tax in brief
Category I and II are pass-through: income is taxed in your hands. Category III pays tax in the fund; you receive post-tax returns.

Cost check: how profits are sharedThe distribution waterfall

Suits you if

  • You have ₹1 crore or more that you will not need for 7 to 10 years.
  • You want a share of the growth that happens before companies list.
  • Your protection and core portfolio are already in place.

Think twice if

  • You may need this money before the fund ends.
  • ₹1 crore is a large share of your net worth.
  • You are not prepared for some investments to fail. Results vary widely between funds.

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • What does the fund invest in, and how did the manager’s earlier funds do?
  • How much will be called, and how often? What if I miss a call?
  • What are the fees, the hurdle and the carry?
  • How long is the fund’s life, and can it be extended?

SpecialiseKnow your products · 07 in depth

Private markets

Where the early growth happens

Indian companies now raise money privately for a decade or more before they list. By the time most investors can buy at the IPO, much of that early growth has already happened. AIFs are how individual investors can take part earlier.

The life of a company, before and after it listsIllustration

13.3 years

from founding to listing, on average, for Indian tech companies that listed in 2025.Orios Venture Partners

$36 billion

invested by private equity and venture capital funds in Indian companies in 2025, across about 1,700 deals.Bain & Company and IVCA

87%

of US companies with over $100 million in revenue are private. Private markets are where much of the economy now sits.S&P Capital IQ, via Apollo

What this means for you

An IPO is often when early investors sell part of their stake to the public. To own a share of a company in its private years, you invest before it lists, through an AIF. That means a long wait, and accepting that some companies never list, or list below their private value.

Private markets

Taking part in private markets

Money committed to AIFsSEBI data, as reported

Which AIFs invest whenBefore a company lists

Category II also covers private credit, which lends to companies, and real estate funds. Many companies never list; funds also exit by selling to other buyers.

Choose the manager with careResults vary widely

Outcomes differ far more from one private-market fund to the next than between funds that invest in listed shares. Ask how long the team has worked together, what happened in its earlier funds, and how it handled difficult years.

Is it for you?Tick what is true

  • ₹1 crore or more that you will not need for 7 to 10 years
  • Protection and a core portfolio already in place
  • Comfortable with no daily price, and with some investments failing
  • Able to meet capital calls on time, for several years

GIFT City

International investing via GIFT IFSC · regulated by IFSCA

GIFT City in Gujarat is home to India’s International Financial Services Centre (IFSC). Resident Indians can invest there in US dollars, within their yearly LRS limit, through entities regulated by IFSCA.

How to recognise it

  • You invest in US dollars. Returns depend on the markets and on the rupee–dollar rate.
  • Uses your LRS limit of USD 2,50,000 per person per financial year, shared with travel, education and gifts.
  • TCS of 20% applies on investment remittances above ₹10 lakh a year. You can set it off against tax or claim a refund.

Often confused with

International funds in rupees. Sold in India in INR, but they can stop taking new money when industry overseas limits are reached.

Foreign broker accounts. Your money sits overseas, under a foreign regulator.

22Facts as of October 2026
08 · GIFT CityGlobalise
At a glanceThe same six facts for every product
Regulator
IFSCA, the regulator for GIFT City. Remittances follow RBI’s Liberalised Remittance Scheme (LRS).
Minimum
Depends on the product: retail funds set their own; PMS from USD 75,000; AIFs from USD 1,50,000 (accredited investors excepted).
Time commitment
Open-ended funds can be redeemed; AIFs run for a fixed term.
Money out
Proceeds are paid in US dollars and can be brought back to your Indian bank account.
Costs
Fund or service fees, plus currency conversion and bank remittance charges.
Tax in brief
Gains are taxable in India for residents. TCS is not an extra tax: it is adjusted against what you owe.

Risk check: the currency effectIllustration only

Suits you if

  • Most of your wealth is in India and you want global diversification.
  • You have goals in dollars: education abroad, travel, overseas property.
  • You prefer an Indian-regulated route and Indian time-zone service.

Think twice if

  • You may need the money soon. Currency swings can hurt in the short term.
  • You have already used most of this year’s LRS limit.
  • You have not planned for TCS holding back cash until you file your return.

Ask before you signTick when answered

  • What exactly does this product invest in, and where?
  • What is the minimum, and what are all costs, including currency conversion?
  • How much of my LRS limit have I used this financial year?
  • How will my gains be taxed?

Know your productsWords to know

Words to know

Terms used in this guide, in plain words.

Accredited investor. Certified as meeting income or wealth tests; some products then have lower minimums.

AMC. Asset management company: the firm that runs a mutual fund’s schemes.

Arbitrage. Buying a share and selling its future at the same time, to capture the small price gap.

Asset cover. The value of assets backing a secured NCD, compared with what is owed.

Capital call. A request for part of the money you committed to an AIF. Also called a drawdown.

Carried interest. The AIF manager’s share of profits above the hurdle.

Cashless claim. The insurer pays a network hospital directly, so you do not pay up front.

Co-payment. The share of each health claim you pay yourself.

Credit rating. An agency’s opinion of how likely a borrower is to pay on time, from AAA to D.

Deductible. The part of a year’s bills that a top-up policy does not pay.

Derivatives. Futures and options: contracts whose value moves with a share or an index.

Exit load. A charge for selling mutual fund units before a set period.

Exposure. How much of a fund moves with the market. A SIF can take it below zero.

Free look. 30 days to return a new insurance policy if it does not suit you.

Hedge. A position that rises when your holdings fall, to cushion the loss.

High-water mark. A performance fee is paid only on gains above the portfolio’s previous peak.

Hurdle rate. The return investors must receive before the manager shares in profits.

IFSCA. International Financial Services Centres Authority, the regulator in GIFT City.

Long-short. Owning shares expected to rise, and betting against those expected to fall.

LRS. Liberalised Remittance Scheme: up to USD 2,50,000 abroad per person, per financial year.

Moratorium. After 5 continuous years of health cover, a claim cannot be refused for non-disclosure, except fraud.

NAV. Net asset value: the price of one mutual fund unit, worked out every business day.

Nominee. The person you name to receive the money from a policy or investment in your absence.

Pass-through. Income taxed in your hands, not in the fund, as for AIF Category I and II.

Portability. Moving a health policy to another insurer while keeping waiting-period credit.

Private markets. Companies and assets not listed on a stock exchange.

Rider. An add-on to an insurance policy, such as cover for critical illness or accidents.

Risk band. The five-level risk label shown for every SIF strategy.

Riskometer. SEBI’s six-level risk label shown on every mutual fund scheme.

SIP. Systematic investment plan: a fixed amount invested at regular intervals.

Sum assured, sum insured. What a life policy pays on a claim; the most a health policy pays in a year.

TCS. Tax collected at source by your bank on large overseas remittances, adjusted against your tax.

TER. Total expense ratio: a fund’s yearly running costs, taken from the NAV.

Venture capital. Money for young, fast-growing private companies, years before they list.

Waiting period. Time after buying health cover before some conditions are covered.
